title: When sakhis differ
hook: traditions sometimes tell the same story in different places; the lesson usually stays the same

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhumia's promises: three small vows that turned a robber around. Your line was promises change us. Did your one promise hold? Day seven hundred forty-three.

At a family dinner, two cousins start telling the same story about their grandfather. One says it happened at the train station. The other says no, it was the market, and it was raining. They argue about the rain for five minutes. Then someone at the end of the table says: does it matter? He gave the man his coat either way. Everyone goes quiet, because that was the whole point of the story. The janamsakhis have dinners like that too. Today: when sakhis differ.
screen: `THE STATION, OR THE MARKET?` → `HE GAVE THE COAT EITHER WAY.` → `THE JANAMSAKHIS HAVE DINNERS LIKE THAT.`

segments.voice: This block began with the janamsakhis and their families: the old Puratan telling, the Bala telling, Miharban's reflective one, the illustrated pages. They don't always agree. A sakhi set in one town in one collection may turn up in another town somewhere else. You've already met it on this path. Tellings place Mardana's death in different places. They differ on what the king did with Bhumia the robber. A detail added in one is missing in another. How do you hold that? Go back to what a sakhi is. We said it at the start: truth carried in the shape of a story. A news report lives or dies by where and when. A sakhi lives by what it teaches. So watch what stays put when the details move. Mardana refuses a tomb, wherever he dies. Bhumia's three promises hold, whatever the king decides. The lesson stays. The differences have their own value, too. Historians compare tellings to learn which material looks older and how stories traveled. That work isn't an attack on the sakhis; it's a kind of care for them. And the differences leave room for humility. A teller who says, in some tellings it was here, in others there, is being honest. Sikh tradition gives its highest authority to the Guru Granth Sahib, not to any janamsakhi, so the stories can differ without the ground moving.
screen: `THE JANAMSAKHIS DON'T ALWAYS AGREE.` · `A SAKHI LIVES BY WHAT IT TEACHES.` · `DETAILS MOVE; THE LESSON STAYS.` · `HONEST ABOUT DIFFERENCES.` · then, large: `THE LESSON STAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold one question open. Pick a story you know two ways: a family story, a news story, a sakhi from this month. Where do the tellings part? For the sit, don't decide which is right. Just let both stand side by side, and ask what they share. Notice what it's like to leave the question open instead of winning it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath. The bell holds the time.
When sakhis differ. Tellings of Nanak's life that place a story in different towns or add different details, while the lesson they carry stays the same.
Your line: the lesson stays. Today, when someone tells a story differently from you, ask what it teaches before you correct the details. Day seven hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Sikh teachers telling a sakhi may note that tellings differ, and the Guru Granth Sahib, not any janamsakhi, is treated as the Guru and final authority.
